title: Curated summary: What counts as a high-oxalate food
text:
What counts as a "high-oxalate" food? Curated summary of the UPMC Urology page "Help Prevent Kidney Stones with a Low-Oxalate Diet".
High oxalate: high-oxalate foods have more than 10 mg of oxalate per serving. (Page section: "Avoid these high-oxalate foods and drinks".)
Moderate oxalate: moderate-oxalate foods have between 2 and 10 mg of oxalate per serving. The page advises no more than two or three servings of these foods per day. (Page section: "Limit these moderate-oxalate foods and drinks".)
Low oxalate: low-oxalate foods have less than 2 mg of oxalate per serving. (Page section: "Enjoy these low-oxalate foods and drinks".)
Serving size: the food lists on that page use servings of 3.5 ounces (100 grams), unless a different amount is noted. (Page section: "A Low-Oxalate Diet Plan".)
Daily total: on a low-oxalate diet, the page says to limit oxalate to 40 to 50 mg each day. (Page section: "A Low-Oxalate Diet Plan".)
Examples the page lists as high-oxalate: nuts, nut butters, spinach, rhubarb, beets, sweet potato, potatoes, black tea, chocolate, wheat bran, and soy milk. (Page section: "Avoid these high-oxalate foods and drinks".)
Your own limit may be different. Follow the diet instructions from your doctor or dietitian.
curation_note: Team-written summary of the linked public page. Every number appears on that page; page sections are named in the text. Checked against snapshot upmc-low-oxalate-diet.
